CP1.title: First checkpoint — Preparing for the search

items.prompt: If ignorance is taken to be a ‘lack of information’, which way can a seeker go astray?
options: He will keep adding information instead of looking at himself
He will stay away from the teacher
items.explanation: If ignorance were only a lack of information, the remedy would be more information. The ignorance of Jñāna Mārga is a mistaken identity, whose remedy is to look at oneself directly.

items.prompt: Desire, fear, comparison and sorrow — what do these four share?
options: All four come from outer circumstances
All four rest on a belief about oneself
All four are only childhood conditioning
items.explanation: All four have one root — taking oneself to be a limited ‘I’.

items.prompt: When does a search become ‘jijñāsā’?
options: When it is satisfied with new information
When it turns back on the one who asks
items.explanation: Curiosity collects; inquiry turns inward.

items.prompt: A seeker is restless because ‘Who am I?’ gets no immediate answer. Which view is most useful?
options: Some questions have to be lived with — keeping the question alive
Accepting that an answer is impossible
items.explanation: Some questions have to be lived with; a hurried answer closes the question.

items.prompt: ‘My feeling changed’ — which distinction does discernment catch in this sentence?
options: Between the feeling and the one who knows it
Between a good and a bad feeling
items.explanation: What changed is the seen; the one to whom the change was known is the seer.

items.prompt: Where is discernment practised?
options: In everyday decisions and reactions too
Only in front of the teacher
items.explanation: Discernment works in daily life too.

items.prompt: What is the basic difference between dispassion and escape?
options: Escape leaves the situation, dispassion lets go of the grip
items.explanation: Dispassion = freedom, not running away.

items.prompt: When does the wish for liberation become a bondage?
options: When it becomes a restless grip and comparison
items.explanation: Even the wish for liberation can become a bondage when it becomes a grip.

items.prompt: In śravaṇa, what does ‘letting the teaching look at you’ mean?
options: Hearing the teaching as a mirror about oneself
items.explanation: Śravaṇa lets the words return to one's own identity.

items.prompt: What does preparing the mind to listen include?
options: Preparing as many questions as possible
items.explanation: A prepared mind is quiet and honest, so the teaching reaches directly.

items.prompt: When is manana considered complete?
options: When the doubt is resolved through experience and reason
When a lot of time has passed
items.explanation: Manana = reflecting on the teaching heard, until doubt ends.

items.prompt: Which sentence best describes the role of reason?
options: Reason clears the way and stops when it reaches the knower
Reason is the enemy of spirituality
items.explanation: Reason removes misconceptions; the knower is not a subject of reasoning.

items.prompt: In nididhyāsana, what is the difference between ‘abiding’ and ‘repeating’?
options: Repeating is a thought; abiding is resting in the awareness that knows the thought
items.explanation: Abiding, not repeating.

items.prompt: How can nididhyāsana happen while cooking in the kitchen?
options: By remaining, while working, as the knowing in which the work is known
items.explanation: On the cushion, and in the kitchen — remaining as the knower in every task.

items.prompt: After neti-neti, what changes in life?
options: Family and work are left behind
One begins to hate the body
The grip of ‘I am just this’ loosens; life goes on
items.explanation: Denying identification, not existence.

items.prompt: After saying ‘not this’ to every layer, what cannot be denied?
options: The knowing that knew every ‘not this’
items.explanation: The knower cannot be denied.

items.concept: the witness is not a thought
items.prompt: ‘I am the witness’ — what is this sentence itself?
options: A thought, which appears in the witness
items.explanation: The witness is not a thought; ‘I am the witness’ is also a thought that comes and goes.

items.prompt: What is the relation between witnessing and compassion?
options: The witness is not coldness; feelings and compassion appear fully within it
items.explanation: Witnessing is not coldness.

CP3.title: Third checkpoint — From experience to the experiencer

items.prompt: What is always true of every experience?
options: It is proof of the Self
items.explanation: Every experience comes and goes.

items.concept: a special experience is not proof
items.prompt: After a spiritual experience, which view is most mature?
options: This too came and will go; let me recognise that in which it came
It must be repeated every day
items.explanation: A special experience is not proof; knowing alone is steady.

items.prompt: Looking at the ‘I’ in ‘I am sad’, what becomes clear?
options: The ‘I’ is also a sense that is being known
items.explanation: The experiencer is also known.

items.prompt: What does the example of deep sleep show about the experiencer?
options: The experiencer is most active in sleep
In sleep the experiencer is absent, yet something remains
Nothing at all remains in sleep
items.explanation: No experiencer in deep sleep, yet knowing remains.

items.prompt: What is the right sequence of the method of self-inquiry?
items.explanation: To whom? · to me · who am I?

items.concept: an answer is a thought too
items.prompt: What is a beautiful answer that comes in self-inquiry?
options: One more thought, known to someone
A new ego to be protected
items.explanation: What remains needs no answer.

items.prompt: Why is self-knowledge called ‘recognition’ rather than ‘acquisition’?
options: Because what is recognised was always there
Because it is only a word
items.explanation: Self-knowledge = recognising what was always present.

items.prompt: What is true of the person after self-knowledge?
options: The person's life goes on; the bondage of a limited identity breaks
items.explanation: The person goes on · the bondage breaks.

items.prompt: In the example of the wave and water, what is the wave?
options: Mithyā — it appears, but depends on water
items.explanation: The world = mithyā, not asatya.

items.prompt: In Jñāna Mārga, what does ‘ātman and Brahman are one’ mean?
options: What is my nature is the one reality of all
Brahman is a small part hidden in the ātman
The two are separate but meet
items.explanation: Brahma-jñāna = the one reality of all = my own nature.

CP4.title: Fourth checkpoint — From silence to natural living

items.concept: the knower is not an object
items.prompt: Why is the knower not known like an object?
options: Because it is the knower itself, by which every object is known
items.explanation: The knower, not an object — and this is not ignorance.

items.prompt: What is the intellect falling silent before the mystery?
items.explanation: The intellect falling silent = maturity.

items.prompt: Why is silence called the ‘background’?
options: Because it happens only at night
Because sounds and thoughts come and go in it
Because it matters less than sound
Because it is hidden behind and never found
items.explanation: Silence = the background.

items.prompt: When emptiness is experienced, what should the next question be?
items.explanation: Who knows the emptiness?

items.prompt: How is the steadiness of the sthitaprajña recognised?
items.explanation: Steadiness = equanimity, not emotionlessness.

items.prompt: In the natural state, what does ‘nothing to gain, become or drop’ mean?
options: Work goes on, but the restless race to complete oneself is gone
items.explanation: Gaining, becoming, dropping — none of it; action goes on, the burden does not.

items.prompt: What is taken to be the root problem in Jñāna Mārga?
items.explanation: Ajñāna = not knowing one's own nature.

items.prompt: An insult stings someone deeply. From the view of Jñāna Mārga, what is useful to look at first?
options: Revenge on the one who insulted
Which image, taken as ‘I’, was hurt
items.explanation: The deepest hurt lands on the image we take to be ourselves.

items.prompt: What is the difference between mumukṣutva (the wish for liberation) and ordinary curiosity?
options: In mumukṣutva the search becomes the priority of one's whole life
Mumukṣutva comes only in old age
items.explanation: When inquiry becomes an intense, central longing for the truth, it is mumukṣutva.

items.prompt: ‘Inquiry means leaving the world’ — why is this a misconception?
options: Because inquiry is an inner search, in the middle of life too
Because leaving the world is hard
Because inquiry is only in children
items.explanation: Inquiry = a true longing to know the truth; leaving the world is not needed for it.

items.prompt: Body, mind and intellect — what does seer-seen discernment say about all three?
options: All three are known, so they are the seen
The intellect is the final seer
items.explanation: What is known is the seen — body, mind, intellect, all of them.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to take discernment as ‘dryness’?
options: Discernment is clarity; tenderness and compassion remain in it
Dryness is the goal of discernment
Discernment has nothing to do with feelings
items.explanation: Discernment = not cleverness, clarity — not dryness.

items.prompt: A father loves his son dearly but does not press him about his career decisions. What is this an example of?
items.explanation: Love without clinging — possible.

items.prompt: What happens when dispassion is taken to mean ‘suppressing desire’?
options: Desires return from being pressed down inside; there is no freedom
items.explanation: Dispassion is not suppression; it is inner freedom from the grip.

items.prompt: What does the sequence of śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana show?
options: Listening, examining, then abiding in the understanding
items.explanation: The teaching heard becomes one's own understanding through manana, and natural through nididhyāsana.

items.prompt: What is the essence of the story of the tenth man?
options: The seeker is the very one being sought
One should stay in a group
items.explanation: ‘Daśamas tvam asi’ — you are the tenth.

items.prompt: What was heard in satsang starts to feel faint by the time one is home. What does manana suggest?
options: Testing it on today's own experience
items.explanation: Understanding tested on experience = seeing.

items.prompt: What is the danger of taking manana to be ‘debate’?
options: Winning the debate becomes the goal, not resolving the doubt
items.explanation: Manana resolves doubt; debate often feeds the ego.

items.prompt: Why is nididhyāsana needed once something has been understood?
options: Because the habit of the old identity returns and has to be seen again
items.explanation: The old identity will return — and be seen again.

items.prompt: Why is it incomplete to take nididhyāsana as ‘concentration’?
options: Concentration rests on an object; nididhyāsana in the knowing in which all objects appear
The two are exactly the same
items.explanation: Myth: nididhyāsana = concentration.

items.prompt: On which principle does the reasoning of neti-neti rest?
options: What is seen is not the seer
The world is full of sorrow
items.explanation: Every ‘not this’ rests on this: what is known is not the knower.

items.prompt: ‘Neti-neti is only an intellectual game’ — why is this a misconception?
options: Because it is seeing every layer directly in one's own experience
Because this game is very difficult
items.explanation: Neti-neti is a distinction made on experience, not just a game of words.

items.prompt: How do you tell the witness from the subtle ego?
options: The witness has no sense of ‘I am special’; the pride of ‘I am the witness’ is a thought
items.explanation: ‘I am the witness’ — can be a subtle ego.

items.prompt: What does witnessing mean when anger arises?
options: Seeing the anger in its own coming and going, not becoming one with it
Letting the anger out on someone
items.explanation: The witness = the awareness in which everything appears, anger too.

items.prompt: What does it mean that the witness is ‘in all three states’?
options: That in which waking, dream and deep sleep are all known does not change
The witness is only in waking
The witness comes only in meditation
items.explanation: The witness in all three states.

items.prompt: What is the difference between experience and knowing?
options: The content of experience changes; knowing is the same in every experience
items.explanation: Experience = comes and goes; knowing = you.

items.prompt: ‘The Self is a special experience’ — why is this a misconception?
options: Because every experience comes and goes, and the Self is that in which experiences come
Because the Self does not exist
items.explanation: Myth 3: the Self = a special experience.

items.prompt: What is the difference between the experiencer and the knower?
options: The experiencer is the sense of ‘it is happening to me’, which is itself known; knowing knows it too
The experiencer is the final truth
items.explanation: The experiencer is also known.

items.prompt: ‘The Self is a small I sitting inside’ — which misconception is this?
options: Taking the Self to be an object or an experiencer
items.explanation: Myth 2: the Self = a small ‘I’ inside.

items.prompt: What do you do if thoughts keep coming during self-inquiry?
options: Make every thought a chance to return to the source with ‘to whom did this come?’
items.explanation: To every thought — ‘to whom?’

items.prompt: What does ‘the seeker = the subject of the search’ mean?
options: What is sought is not an object separate from the seeker
items.explanation: When the seeker becomes the subject of the search, what remains needs no answer.

items.prompt: Why is it a misconception to use self-inquiry as a way to escape the world?
options: Because self-inquiry happens in the middle of life, with every thought
items.explanation: Myth 4: escaping the world.

items.prompt: Which statement about self-knowledge is most exact?
options: It is the recognition of what was always present
It is the result of reading books
It is the achievement of a special person
items.explanation: Recognition, not a new experience; not an achievement.

items.prompt: ‘Reading books is enough for self-knowledge’ — what is left out?
options: Manana and direct recognition in one's own experience
items.explanation: Myth 4: just reading books.

items.prompt: Satya, mithyā and asatya — where does the world belong?
items.explanation: The world = mithyā, not asatya.

items.prompt: What is the mistake in taking Brahman to be ‘a power sitting in the sky’?
options: It makes Brahman a separate object, while it is the one reality of all
items.explanation: Myth 2: a power sitting in the sky.

items.prompt: How are ‘ātman = Brahman’ and ‘I am not the body’ connected?
options: The knower that is not the body is the very one reality of all
The first is only in scripture, the second in experience
items.explanation: The ‘I’ recognised through discernment is seen by knowledge of Brahman as the reality of all.

items.prompt: What is the difference between unknowability and ignorance?
options: Unknowability is the nature of the knower; ignorance is a mistake about one's identity
items.explanation: Ajñeyatā = the knower is not an object · not ignorance.

items.prompt: ‘Unknowability means that “I” will disappear’ — why is this a misconception?
options: Because the knower is not an object, yet not absent either — it always is
items.explanation: Myth 4: ‘I’ will disappear.

items.prompt: What is the difference between silence (mauna) and quiet?
options: Quiet is the absence of sound; silence is that in which sound also appears
items.explanation: Silence = the background.

items.prompt: How can silence be recognised amid crowds and noise?
options: By seeing the sounds come and go in the background in which they appear
items.explanation: Silence is present as the background even while sound is there.

items.prompt: What happens inside a sthitaprajña when praised?
options: Praise comes, feels pleasant, but does not become an identity
items.explanation: Equanimity: living without wavering in pleasure and pain.

items.prompt: ‘The sthitaprajña does not care about anyone’ — why is this a misconception?
options: Because equanimity is not indifference; care and compassion remain
Because the sthitaprajña worries about everyone
items.explanation: Myth 1: not caring.

items.prompt: What is the relation between nididhyāsana and sthitaprajña life?
options: Through nididhyāsana understanding becomes natural, which shows effortlessly in sthitaprajña life
items.explanation: Abiding → natural → natural living.

items.prompt: Neti-neti, witnessing and self-inquiry — in which one direction do all three point?
options: Toward the knower, which is not known like an object
items.explanation: All three methods turn back from the seen to the seer.

items.prompt: What does completing this course prove?
options: Understanding of the curriculum, so that it can be examined further in nididhyāsana
items.explanation: Completing the course only shows understanding; no spiritual attainment is certified.
